Google Calendar add-on

A contribution graph for your calendar

Every day of the year as a square, shaded by how many hours you were actually in meetings. Calendar tells you what is next; this tells you what the last year looked like.

How it worksView source

Free and open source, MIT licensed. Not yet on the Google Workspace Marketplace — you can run your own copy today.

Why it exists

Calendar has no memory

Calendar is good at the next hour and bad at the last year. It cannot tell you whether February really was worse than October, whether your Tuesdays have quietly filled up, or whether the term you remember as brutal actually was.

This counts the hours and shows you the shape.

Method

What counts as a meeting

A number you cannot trust is worse than no number, so the counting rules are strict and stated.

You have to be in it

An event counts if you organised it, or you were invited and did not decline. Items sitting on a shared team calendar with no guest list are ignored unless you created them.

Overlaps merge

Triple-booked from 9 to 10 counts as one hour, not three. The graph measures time you spent, not invitations you received.

Not-really-meetings are dropped

Out-of-office, working location, birthdays, all-day entries, and anything longer than fourteen hours never reach the total.

Privacy

Your calendar never leaves Google

There is no server, because there is nothing for a server to do. The script runs inside your own Google account, reads the calendars you chose, and draws the result.

Event titles, locations, and guest lists are read in memory to work out durations and are never written anywhere. Only the hours-per-day totals are kept, and only in a cache that expires within the hour.

Read the privacy policy
  • No analytics, telemetry, tracking or advertising.
  • No data sold, shared, or disclosed to third parties.
  • No profiling, and nothing used to train machine-learning models.
  • Read-only access — the add-on cannot create, edit or delete events.

Getting started

How it works

  1. 01

    Open the add-on

    In Google Calendar, click the Meeting load icon in the right-hand sidebar.

  2. 02

    Choose your calendars

    Pick which calendars to count. Most people want their primary one; add a team calendar if your real meetings live there.

  3. 03

    Set where your year starts

    The year splits on a date you choose, so a school or fiscal year lines up properly instead of being cut at 1 January.

  4. 04

    Open the graph

    The sidebar card shows your headline numbers. One click opens the full graph as an overlay, without leaving Calendar.

Running your own copy takes an Apps Script project and about ten minutes — the repository README has the full sequence. Self-hosted copies show Google's “hasn't verified this app” screen on first authorisation, which is expected for an unverified script.

Support

Getting help

Something counted wrong, or the graph looks off? Both are worth reporting — the counting rules are the part most likely to disagree with how you actually work.
